title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers

paper.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers

sections.heading: 1   Introduction
sections.text: Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with a computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As a result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on a 256 × 256 256\times 256 image, reducing the patch size from 16 × 16 16\times 16 to 8 × 8 8\times 8 increases the token count from 256 to 1,024, making the quadratic term of dense attention 16 × 16\times larger. Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence [ 34 ] . Multiscale systems move detail to extra stages or detailer heads [ 52 , 9 , 22 ] , and efficient-attention methods shorten the sequence with generic patterns—windows, selected global tokens, or learned sparsity [ 36 , 4 , 31 , 55 ] . Spectral Forcing brings in frequency structure, but only to filter the noisy input; its tokens remain spatial patches [ 19 ] . Across the pixel-space generators discussed above, output detail remains tied to a spatial patch grid, even when communication is compressed or restricted. Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. A token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while a token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what a token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can a token’s output role also determine how it should communicate? SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations: Read , Allocate , and Route . Read forms a grid of spatial anchors that collect input evidence. Allocate expands each anchor into K K indexed slots, with each slot assigned a disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. A spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add a local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure 2 illustrates this design. Figure 2: SpecSlot data flow. Each anchor expands into K K slots. G blocks process lowest-radial slot-0 carriers across anchors with context states; L blocks mix all slots within each anchor. The final slot states decode a lapped-DCT spectral base and an anchor-aligned spatial correction, summed in pixel space. This representation exposes two separate allocation variables. W W controls the density of spatial anchors, while K K controls the spectral subdivision at each anchor. The total number of slots grows with W ​ K WK , but the global image sequence contains only W W carriers. A fixed token budget can therefore be allocated either to denser spatial anchors or to finer spectral roles without forcing both to increase together. This turns tokenization from a single patch-size choice into an explicit quality–compute allocation problem. Our contributions are: • We introduce an indexed W × K W\times K representation in which spatial anchors collect input evidence and slots receive disjoint spectral coefficient groups. The split exposes anchor density and coefficient subdivision as separate allocation variables, and the same slot states also decode a local pixel correction. • We define carrier-routed global–global–local–local (GGLL) attention from the slot index: one lowest-radial carrier per anchor enters global blocks, and all slots enter anchor-local blocks, so the global sequence contains W W carriers rather than W ​ K WK slots. • On ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512, SpecSlot provides two measured quality–compute operating points between JiT’s low-cost and high-cost settings. At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Larger output windows cover more pixels while the global sequence remains fixed; the larger improvement over JiT-CM is consistent with this within-anchor allocation. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot likewise surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

sections.heading: Diffusion and pixel-space generation.
sections.text: Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis [ 24 , 47 , 14 ] . Rectified flow turns the same idea into a straight noise-to-data path [ 35 ] . Latent diffusion moved this process into the latent space of a separately trained autoencoder, and improved autoencoders continue to strengthen this line [ 17 , 45 , 54 ] . DiT, U-ViT, and SiT showed that plain Transformers scale reliably in this setting [ 41 , 3 , 37 ] . Pixel-space generation removes the autoencoder, but then asks the model to process the full-resolution state. This line has followed several routes: Simple Diffusion and Hourglass DiT reduce the state internally, cascaded models and PixelFlow distribute generation across resolutions, and JiT shows that a direct large-patch Transformer can remain a strong pixel-space baseline [ 27 , 11 , 25 , 8 , 34 ] . Detail recovery is then assigned to extra components: PixelDiT adds a pixel-level DiT, DiP adds a detailer head, HyperDiT connects coarse and fine flows, and PixNerd decodes patch tokens with a neural field [ 52 , 9 , 22 , 50 ] . These designs differ in where the compute goes, but share one premise: a token is a spatial patch, so finer detail and wider communication stay tied to the same spatial grid. SpecSlot complements this line with a single-backbone allocation: indexed slots carry fixed output and communication roles, so detail can be subdivided without making every output token global.

sections.heading: Frequency structure and transform-domain generation.
sections.text: Frequency offers a complementary view of this problem. It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. In the first line, inverse heat dissipation, wavelet models, sparse transform codes, and DCTdiff change the representation or process used for generation [ 44 , 21 , 43 , 39 , 40 ] . In the second, VAR and NFIG organize generation by scale or frequency, while Spectral Forcing and Frequency-Forcing use frequency-related conditioning or guidance; Latent Forcing instead reorders the trajectory with a semantic auxiliary stream [ 49 , 29 , 19 , 2 , 16 ] . Focal frequency loss reweights spectral errors, and Fourier-space analyses characterize diffusion without changing the denoiser [ 32 , 18 ] . Recent architectural methods make frequency roles part of the denoiser itself: DiMSUM alternates spatial and wavelet-subband processing, while DeCo assigns low and high frequencies to a DiT and a separate pixel decoder [ 42 , 38 ] . Together these works show several ways for frequency to shape representation or generation, but the cited lines do not use fixed spectral groups as both per-token output ownership and communication eligibility within one pixel-space backbone. SpecSlot keeps the state, target, and loss in pixel space; fixed, disjoint DCT groups give slots spectral roles, and the role index also determines which slots communicate globally.

sections.heading: Visual tokenization and allocation.
sections.text: Vision Transformers tokenize an image into a spatial patch grid [ 15 ] , and NaViT extends this idea to variable resolutions [ 12 ] . This line reduces sequence work by changing how many spatial tokens are retained or processed at each step: ToMe merges similar tokens, SparseDiT prunes them, DyDiT++ reschedules computation across denoising time and space, variable-length tokenization learns a global merge, and FlexiDiT spends fewer tokens at easier steps [ 5 , 6 , 53 , 33 , 1 ] . The spatial patch remains the allocation unit, so detail and communication stay coupled to the same grid. SpecSlot adds a second, spectral axis: each of W W anchors owns K K slots with disjoint coefficient groups, making the fixed budget N = W ​ K N{=}WK an explicit split between anchor density and spectral subdivision.

sections.heading: Global-local and sparse communication.
sections.text: The communication literature provides the other half of the problem by restricting how tokens exchange information. Swin uses local windows with shifted boundaries, Longformer combines local windows with a few global tokens, and Perceiver routes information through a small latent bottleneck [ 36 , 4 , 31 ] . In pixel-space generation, RINs exchange information through learned interface states, while trainable sparse attention and PixSGR learn or select interaction patterns from the data [ 30 , 55 , 51 ] . These approaches provide useful local or global topologies, but do not tie communication eligibility to a fixed spectral output role. SpecSlot fixes the graph from the allocation: one lowest-frequency slot per anchor is the global carrier, and all slots interact locally, so cross-anchor communication is spent on the role that also carries the low-frequency scaffold.

sections.heading: 3   Methodology
sections.text: SpecSlot organizes pixel-space generation around one idea: tokenization as allocation—assigning each token a fixed output role and dividing a fixed token budget between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global attention is then spent only on the role that needs it; the rectified-flow state, target, and loss remain in pixel space.

sections.heading: 3.2   SpecSlot Architecture
sections.text: Figure 3: SpecSlot allocation. A patch grid spends all N N tokens in one global sequence; splitting N = W ​ K N{=}WK into W W spatial anchors and K K spectral slots keeps global attention at W W carriers. Why is allocation needed? In a patch-grid model, adding finer detail means shrinking the patch, and the global sequence grows with it; the two cannot be adjusted separately. Prior designs keep the spatial patch as the only allocation unit. SpecSlot instead introduces the missing variables, forming W W spatial anchors and expanding each anchor into K K indexed slots (Figure 3 ): N \displaystyle N = W K , L = 2 s , \displaystyle=WK,\qquad L=2s, (4) W \displaystyle W = ( H / s ) 2 , E = L 2 K = 4 ​ H 2 N . \displaystyle=(H/s)^{2},\qquad E=\frac{L^{2}}{K}=\frac{4H^{2}}{N}. The budget splits into W W anchors that read the input and K K slots per anchor that divide the output; each slot owns an equal share E E of the coefficients per channel, with s s the input cell side and L L the output window side. The two variables act separately: W W sets how densely the input is read, and K K how finely the output is divided. At fixed N N , anchor density trades directly against spectral subdivision, and output detail can grow with K K while the global sequence stays at W W carriers. Equal N N does not imply equal cost, since communication and projection scale differently with the split. Three operations implement this allocation, as shown in Figure 2 : Read collects each anchor’s input evidence, Allocate assigns each slot a fixed output role, and Route lets the role decide communication.

sections.text: The same slot states can also be read out directly in pixel space. A second head adds an anchor-aligned correction alongside the spectral base: slot k k writes tile k k of a deterministic row-major K h × K w K_{h}\times K_{w} tiling ( K h ​ K w = K K_{h}K_{w}{=}K ) of its anchor cell (four 8 × 8 8\times 8 quadrants for K = 4 K{=}4 , s = 16 s{=}16 ). These projections are slot-specific and zero-initialized, so training starts from a pure spectral model. The correction adds output parameters but no token states or attention edges. Radial ownership applies only to the spectral base; the spatial term is a pixel readout with no frequency assignment. The two terms express the same prediction in different bases, and Section 6.1 finds their content complementary. sections.heading: 3.2.3   Route: Carrier and Local Attention
sections.text: The third question is who needs to communicate globally. Sending every slot through global attention would make the global quadratic cost grow with K K —reintroducing exactly the coupling between output detail and communication cost that the slot allocation set out to remove. The spectral roles suggest a cheaper split: the lowest radial group holds the broad structure that benefits from cross-anchor exchange, while finer groups are increasingly local; its signal also overtakes the noise earliest in the flow (Section 6.2 ). SpecSlot therefore routes by role: the owner of the lowest radial group, slot 0 0 , is the carrier and the only slot entering the global stage; all K K slots then mix locally within their anchor. Since global and local blocks alternate, the carrier brings global information into its anchor and takes local detail back into the next global stage. Let 𝐙 ∈ ℝ W × K × d \mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times K\times d} be the slot tensor and 𝐘 ∈ ℝ C × d \mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d} the C = 32 C{=}32 context states formed from the class embedding. Class context appears only in the global group. Non-carrier slots traverse the six local blocks, context states the six global ones, and carriers all twelve. Measured GFLOPs include the full execution and decoder, not only these terms. Because W W and K K can be varied independently, their effects on quality and compute can be measured separately.

sections.heading: Models and training.
sections.text: We train class-conditional models on ImageNet-1K [ 13 ] and report results at ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512. Unless stated otherwise, our models use the W ​ 256 W256 anchor grid of Section 3 with B = 1536 B{=}1536 , where B B is the input-projection width; we write SpecSlot-K2 and SpecSlot-K4 for the two allocations. ImageNet-256 training lasts 120 epochs at effective batch 512, and the aligned models share the full training recipe.

The ImageNet-512 control JiT-CM/141G uses the corresponding 16 × 16 16\times 16 tokenizer at width 600 (141.21 GFLOPs); we write JiT-CM for the resolution-matched control in what follows.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: We test whether the allocation and routing design transfers from class labels to text conditions. We train at 256 × 256 256\times 256 on a mixture of the BLIP3o long-caption and short-caption shards [ 7 ] and JourneyDB shards [ 48 ] . A frozen OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 encoder [ 10 ] and a trainable 32-query adapter provide the denoiser context. SpecSlot reads this context through its carrier states during the global route, while local blocks continue to process image slots; JiT uses the same text encoder and adapter. We retain the ImageNet rectified-flow objective, optimizer, and EMA; the complete training contract is in Appendix Table 9 . Evaluation uses the 50-step Heun sampler with CFG 4.0 for SpecSlot and 2.9 for JiT. Table 2 reports the results.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Transferred to text conditioning, SpecSlot attains the highest DPG-Bench score, improving over both JiT baselines at 40.6% lower forward cost than the stronger JiT-B/8 (Table 2 ). On GenEval it improves over JiT-B/16, while JiT-B/8 remains the quality leader at 1.7 × 1.7\times the forward cost—the same quality–compute trade-off as on ImageNet-256. This transfer requires no T2I-specific change to the SpecSlot architecture or training objective. sections.heading: 5.1.1   Anchor Density and Coefficient Subdivision
sections.text: Both allocation axes trade compute for quality, but they are not interchangeable: W W improves the read, K K refines the write (Table 4 ). sections.heading: 5.1.2   Input and Output Representations
sections.text: At the same spectral output, spatial input surpasses frequency input, and the dual-basis hybrid achieves the best FID: 6.59, a further 0.40 below the best single-basis variant at 6.99, without adding tokens or cross-anchor attention edges (Table 4 (b)). This margin indicates that the two output bases are not redundant: the spatial correction supplies structure that the spectral base alone misses. Section 6.1 localizes this complementarity over the flow and across frequency bands.

sections.heading: 5.1.3   Carrier Routing
sections.text: To test routing at a fixed forward budget, we train a full-global control (Dense-global-CM) on the same W ​ 256 / K ​ 4 W256/K4 configuration, replacing the carrier/local schedule with 12 full-global blocks over all 1,024 image slots; its hidden width is 560, matching the measured GGLL forward cost. GGLL is both better and faster than this control at essentially identical FLOPs (Table 3 ). Full-global attention reaches a lower FID but at 74.8% higher cost and lower throughput. The carrier design therefore targets the intermediate, attention-constrained regime, saving 42.8% of the full-global cost. GLGL keeps the same carrier set and global budget but alternates the global/local order; its FID degrades at identical compute, showing that block order affects performance under this fixed carrier set. Section 6.2 provides a possible motivation for early global processing: the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest in the flow.

sections.heading: 7   Conclusion
sections.text: SpecSlot recasts tokenization as allocation: a fixed token budget is split between anchor density and spectral subdivision, while global attention is assigned by role. On ImageNet-256, it reaches a comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models a new way to trade detail for communication.

sections.heading: Appendix E Additional Mechanistic Diagnostics
sections.text: This appendix collects measurements that probe how SpecSlot uses its explicit roles. Unless stated otherwise, a probe loads a checkpoint and intervenes on its states without updating any parameter; these results characterize representation and communication rather than claim end-to-end quality gains. For the route probe, the intervention is made inside the shared Transformer after slot formation and before the output head, so its interpretation concerns the spectral-slot/GGLL submodule rather than a particular output basis.

We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost. Project Page: https://yangjiongfan.site/specslot/ GitHub: https://github.com/JiongfanYang/SpecSlot Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/Gokottaw434/SpecSlot Figure 1: Text-to-image samples generated by SpecSlot. More samples with prompts are shown in Appendix Figure 10 . 1 Introduction Pixel-space generative models learn directly from noise to pixels, eliminating the separately trained autoencoder and its compression bottleneck. This simplicity, however, comes with a computational cost: the full-resolution image must be represented as Transformer tokens. Most pixel-space Transformers use one token per spatial patch, so the patch grid simultaneously determines what the model reads, what each token predicts, and how many tokens participate in global attention. As a result, finer image detail directly increases attention cost: on a 256 × 256 256\times 256 image, reducing the patch size from 16 × 16 16\times 16 to 8 × 8 8\times 8 increases the token count from 256 to 1,024, making the quadratic term of dense attention 16 × 16\times larger. Existing methods address this cost from different directions, but largely retain the coupling between output detail and token communication. JiT routes every patch token through the global sequence [ 34 ] . Multiscale systems move detail to extra stages or detailer heads [ 52 , 9 , 22 ] , and efficient-attention methods shorten the sequence with generic patterns—windows, selected global tokens, or learned sparsity [ 36 , 4 , 31 , 55 ] . Spectral Forcing brings in frequency structure, but only to filter the noisy input; its tokens remain spatial patches [ 19 ] . Across the pixel-space generators discussed above, output detail remains tied to a spatial patch grid, even when communication is compressed or restricted. Our key observation is that finer detail does not necessarily require proportionally more global communication: in the frequency domain, low-frequency structure carries broad image organization and benefits from long-range exchange, while fine detail is largely local. A token carrying broad structure therefore stands to gain from exchanging with the whole image, while a token carrying fine detail mostly does not. Yet in existing designs, what a token communicates is fixed by where it sits, not by what it produces. Can a token’s output role also determine how it should communicate? SpecSlot builds on this idea by making output roles explicit and using them to control communication. It organizes computation around three operations: Read , Allocate , and Route . Read forms a grid of spatial anchors that collect input evidence. Allocate expands each anchor into K K indexed slots, with each slot assigned a disjoint radial group of DCT coefficients. Route then uses these spectral roles to decide communication: only the slot assigned the lowest-frequency group from each anchor enters the global stage, while all slots interact locally within the anchor. This separates fine-grained output representation from the length of the global sequence. A spatial head further reuses the same slot states to add a local correction to the spectral prediction, without introducing additional tokens. Figure 2 illustrates this design. Figure 2: SpecSlot data flow. Each anchor expands into K K slots. G blocks process lowest-radial slot-0 carriers across anchors with context states; L blocks mix all slots within each anchor. The final slot states decode a lapped-DCT spectral base and an anchor-aligned spatial correction, summed in pixel space. This representation exposes two separate allocation variables. W W controls the density of spatial anchors, while K K controls the spectral subdivision at each anchor. The total number of slots grows with W ​ K WK , but the global image sequence contains only W W carriers. A fixed token budget can therefore be allocated either to denser spatial anchors or to finer spectral roles without forcing both to increase together. This turns tokenization from a single patch-size choice into an explicit quality–compute allocation problem. Our contributions are: • We introduce an indexed W × K W\times K representation in which spatial anchors collect input evidence and slots receive disjoint spectral coefficient groups. The split exposes anchor density and coefficient subdivision as separate allocation variables, and the same slot states also decode a local pixel correction. • We define carrier-routed global–global–local–local (GGLL) attention from the slot index: one lowest-radial carrier per anchor enters global blocks, and all slots enter anchor-local blocks, so the global sequence contains W W carriers rather than W ​ K WK slots. • On ImageNet-256 and ImageNet-512, SpecSlot provides two measured quality–compute operating points between JiT’s low-cost and high-cost settings. At ImageNet-512, W256/K4 lowers FID by 2.84 over our FLOPs-matched JiT control (JiT-CM) with 3.9% fewer GFLOPs, and trails JiT-B/16 by 0.69 FID at 38.2% lower cost. Larger output windows cover more pixels while the global sequence remains fixed; the larger improvement over JiT-CM is consistent with this within-anchor allocation. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot likewise surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost. 2 Related Work Diffusion and pixel-space generation. Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and provide the iterative foundation of modern image synthesis [ 24 , 47 , 14 ] . Rectified flow turns the same idea into a straight noise-to-data path [ 35 ] . Latent diffusion moved this process into the latent space of a separately trained autoencoder, and improved autoencoders continue to strengthen this line [ 17 , 45 , 54 ] . DiT, U-ViT, and SiT showed that plain Transformers scale reliably in this setting [ 41 , 3 , 37 ] . Pixel-space generation removes the autoencoder, but then asks the model to process the full-resolution state. This line has followed several routes: Simple Diffusion and Hourglass DiT reduce the state internally, cascaded models and PixelFlow distribute generation across resolutions, and JiT shows that a direct large-patch Transformer can remain a strong pixel-space baseline [ 27 , 11 , 25 , 8 , 34 ] . Detail recovery is then assigned to extra components: PixelDiT adds a pixel-level DiT, DiP adds a detailer head, HyperDiT connects coarse and fine flows, and PixNerd decodes patch tokens with a neural field [ 52 , 9 , 22 , 50 ] . These designs differ in where the compute goes, but share one premise: a token is a spatial patch, so finer detail and wider communication stay tied to the same spatial grid. SpecSlot complements this line with a single-backbone allocation: indexed slots carry fixed output and communication roles, so detail can be subdivided without making every output token global. Frequency structure and transform-domain generation. Frequency offers a complementary view of this problem. It has entered generative modeling through the state or forward process, through generation order or conditioning, and through the training objective or analysis. In the first line, inverse heat dissipation, wavelet models, sparse transform codes, and DCTdiff change the representation or process used for generation [ 44 , 21 , 43 , 39 , 40 ] . In the second, VAR and NFIG organize generation by scale or frequency, while Spectral Forcing and Frequency-Forcing use frequency-related conditioning or guidance; Latent Forcing instead reorders the trajectory with a semantic auxiliary stream [ 49 , 29 , 19 , 2 , 16 ] . Focal frequency loss reweights spectral errors, and Fourier-space analyses characterize diffusion without changing the denoiser [ 32 , 18 ] . Recent architectural methods make frequency roles part of the denoiser itself: DiMSUM alternates spatial and wavelet-subband processing, while DeCo assigns low and high frequencies to a DiT and a separate pixel decoder [ 42 , 38 ] . Together these works show several ways for frequency to shape representation or generation, but the cited lines do not use fixed spectral groups as both per-token output ownership and communication eligibility within one pixel-space backbone. SpecSlot keeps the state, target, and loss in pixel space; fixed, disjoint DCT groups give slots spectral roles, and the role index also determines which slots communicate globally. Visual tokenization and allocation. Vision Transformers tokenize an image into a spatial patch grid [ 15 ] , and NaViT extends this idea to variable resolutions [ 12 ] . This line reduces sequence work by changing how many spatial tokens are retained or processed at each step: ToMe merges similar tokens, SparseDiT prunes them, DyDiT++ reschedules computation across denoising time and space, variable-length tokenization learns a global merge, and FlexiDiT spends fewer tokens at easier steps [ 5 , 6 , 53 , 33 , 1 ] . The spatial patch remains the allocation unit, so detail and communication stay coupled to the same grid. SpecSlot adds a second, spectral axis: each of W W anchors owns K K slots with disjoint coefficient groups, making the fixed budget N = W ​ K N{=}WK an explicit split between anchor density and spectral subdivision. Global-local and sparse communication. The communication literature provides the other half of the problem by restricting how tokens exchange information. Swin uses local windows with shifted boundaries, Longformer combines local windows with a few global tokens, and Perceiver routes information through a small latent bottleneck [ 36 , 4 , 31 ] . In pixel-space generation, RINs exchange information through learned interface states, while trainable sparse attention and PixSGR learn or select interaction patterns from the data [ 30 , 55 , 51 ] . These approaches provide useful local or global topologies, but do not tie communication eligibility to a fixed spectral output role. SpecSlot fixes the graph from the allocation: one lowest-frequency slot per anchor is the global carrier, and all slots interact locally, so cross-anchor communication is spent on the role that also carries the low-frequency scaffold. 3 Methodology SpecSlot organizes pixel-space generation around one idea: tokenization as allocation—assigning each token a fixed output role and dividing a fixed token budget between anchor density and spectral subdivision. On ImageNet-256, it reaches a comparable final FID to the FLOPs-matched JiT control and descends faster early in training; on ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over that control and approaches JiT-B/16 at 38% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, the same design surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench (62.21 vs. 61.15) at 40.6% lower forward cost. These results show that, in the evaluated pixel-space settings, output detail and global-communication cost can be decoupled through tokenization. Our diagnostics find the lowest-radial role is recovered earliest, supporting its use as the carrier. Allocation gives pixel-space models a new way to trade detail for communication.
